Noisy or outlier samples are assigned very low membership scores due to their low local density and inconsistent neighborhood structure. Consequently, their contribution to both the empirical loss and the complexity term becomes negligible. This results in a tighter bound and improved generalization performance. Hence, the proposed RD-IFTSVM model ensures theoretical robustness in the presence of noise and outliers.

The time complexity of the proposed model is analyzed using the big O notation. Let the total count of the training patterns be N , comprising n 1 number of positive class instances and n 2 number of negative class instances. The class IR is computed as n 2 /n 1, considering the positive class as the minority class. To compute the membership degree using relative density, the distance of each training point in the majority class to its kth neighbor must be calculated, which requires a complexity of O(n 2). The evaluation of the nonmembership function is primarily dominated by the computation of pairwise distances within the majority class, leading to a time complexity of O(n2). Also, the complexity of solving the two QPPs in TSVM is O(n3) + O(n3). Therefore, the overall time complexity of 1 2 the proposed method is (IR 3 + 1)O(n3 ) + O(n2 ) + O(n 2). In

comparison, the ACFTSVM model [26] computes membership values through affinity calculations with a time complexity of O(n 2 × n SVs ), where n SVs denotes the number of support vectors in the SVDD model. In addition, class probability estimation is performed using kernel k-nearest neighbors, which incurs a complexity of O(k × N × n 2), where k is the number of nearest neighbors. Consequently, the overall time complexity of ACFTSVM is (IR 3 + 1)O(n3 1 ) + O(n 2 × ) + O(k × N × n 2). On the other hand, the CGFTSVM n SVs model [27] calculates generalized bell-shaped membership values and class probabilities for majority class samples each with a time complexity of O(n 2) and solves the QPPs with a complexity of (1 + IR 3)O(n3). Therefore, the proposed method achieves lower computational complexity than ACFTSVM while remains comparable to that of CGFTSVM.

To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed RD- IFTSVM, we conducted the experiments on 30 imbalanced datasets from KEEL [33] and UCI [34] repositories. We compare the performance of the proposed method with several stateof-the-art techniques, including SVM-SMOTE [3], TSVM [8], IFTPSVM [12], IFTSVM-ID [24], IFW-LSTSVM [13], ACFTSVM [26], and CGFTSVM [27]. The method SVM- SMOTE first utilizes the SMOTE technique [18] to oversample the minority class and then trains an SVM on the balanced dataset. The statistical information of the datasets is presented in Table S-I of the Supplementary Material.

All experiments are conducted using Python on a highperformance supercomputer equipped with an Intel Xeon Platinum 8268 processor. We employ a tenfold cross-validation approach combined with a grid search method to determine the optimal hyperparameters. The dataset is initially divided into ten equal folds, where each fold serves once as the validation data while the other nine folds are used for training the model. In the cross-validation process, the validation data serve as the testing data and the average area under curve (AUC) score is calculated to assess the model generalization performance. The optimal values of the hyperparameters are evaluated from the selected sets, based on the highest average AUC scores. The penalty and regularization parameters in all models are configured as C 1 = C 3 and C 2 = C 4 to streamline the computational process and are selected from the set {10−2, 10−1, . . . , 103}. In the nonlinear case, we utilize the Gaussian kernel (K(x 1 , x 2) = exp{−σ(cid:3)x 1 − x 2 (cid:3)2}), with the parameter σ > 0 selected from the set {2−2, 2−1, . . . , 25}. We evaluate the efficacy of the proposed RD-IFTSVM by comparing its performance against several state-of-the-art techniques on 30 imbalanced datasets. The computed AUC values, along with the standard deviation (SD), are presented in Tables I and II for the linear and nonlinear kernels, respectively. The highest AUC values for each dataset among all classifiers are highlighted in bold. The corresponding optimal parameters for the linear and Gaussian kernels are provided in Tables S-II and S-III of the Supplementary Material, respectively, while the computational time is presented in Tables S-IV and S-V of the Supplementary Material. The proposed RD-IFTSVM exhibited superior generalization performance on a majority of datasets, outperforming existing methods in 22 out of 30 cases with a linear kernel and in 23 out of 30 cases with the Gaussian kernel. Furthermore, the proposed technique yields an average AUC of 91.63% on all benchmark datasets, surpassing the performance of all existing classifiers in the linear case. This is followed by CGFTSVM with average AUC (90.45%), IFW-LSTSVM (88.62%), ACFTSVM (88.39%), IFTSVM-ID (88.29%), IFTPSVM (86.42%), SVM-SMOTE (83.92%), and TSVM (83.85%). content: To further assess the impact of each component of the proposed RDNM-based membership function separately, we perform ablation studies on five randomly selected benchmark datasets using both linear and nonlinear kernels. In these studies, we meticulously exclude or tweak the components of the model to examine their influence on performance. We examined different combinations of these components: our relative densitybased membership function, the proposed nonmembership function, the traditional distance-based membership function [10], and the nonmembership function based on local density [11]. The results presented in Table S-X of the Supplementary Material demonstrate that the integration of the proposed nonmembership function consistently yields superior performance compared to the local density-based nonmembership approach in both the cases. This illustrates that the new nonmembership approach enhances the model’s capability to classify training patterns adequately by capturing the global information of the datasets. Furthermore, we observe that using a relative density-based membership function leads to improved classifier performance compared to traditional membership approaches.

The result of these studies affirms that each component of the proposed method contributes to its outstanding performance, further emphasizing the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

This section investigates the sensitivity of the proposed RD- IFTSVM to its key parameters C 1 , C 2, and σ, and analyzes how variations in these parameters influence the overall performance of the model. In the first experiment, we set C 1 = C 2 = C and evaluate the AUC values on the three benchmark datasets (glass1, vehicle1, and spect) for C ∈ {10−3, 10−2, . . . , 102}. The evaluation is performed using both linear and nonlinear kernels, with the results visualized in Figs. S-1 and S-2 of the Supplementary Material, respectively. These figures exhibit a declining trend in performance as the parameter C increases to larger values. In the second experiment, we simultaneously vary C 1 and C 2 along the x-axis and y-axis, respectively, while evaluating the AUC value on the z-axis. This experiment is conducted across four datasets: ecoli4, monk2, poker9vs7,

and cleveland0vs4 using linear and Gaussian kernels. The corresponding graphs are shown in Fig. 3. Finally, we investigate the impact of the kernel width parameter σ on the model’s generalization performance. The parameter σ varies across the set {2−1, 20, . . . , 25}, and the corresponding AUC values are evaluated on four imbalanced datasets (new-thyroid1, pima, yeast1vs7, and yeast05679vs4). The results in Fig. S-3 of the Supplementary Material illustrate that the proposed RD-IFTSVM consistently outperforms the existing methods, CGFTSVM, ACFTSVM, and IFTSVM-ID, across different values of σ. It is important to note that in all experiments, the remaining parameters are fixed at their optimal

This statistical method ranks the classifiers based on the absolute differences in their AUC performance while preserving the sign of these differences. Let R+ and R− denote the sum of the ranks for the positive and negative differences, respectively. If the minimum of the two calculated sums is less than or equal to the critical value at α = 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis. In our case for n = 30, the critical value is 137. In this section, we apply the proposed RD-IFTSVM to skin lesion classification [36] to demonstrate its applicability to real-world data. Skin lesions are diseases that arise from the aberrant proliferation of skin cells, potentially leading to skin cancer and other severe health complications. The visual characteristics of skin lesions, including diverse shapes, sizes,

Fig. 4. Sample images representing the two skin lesion from the HAM10000 dataset.

colors, and indistinct boundaries, pose a significant challenge for machine learning classification. Accurate classification and early detection of these lesions are crucial for effective diagnosis and treatment. Therefore, we utilize the proposed technique to detect skin lesions, thereby contributing to improve patient health outcomes.

This study utilizes the publicly available HAM10000 dataset [37], comprising 10000 dermatoscopic images accessible through the International Skin Imaging Collaboration Archive. The dataset encompasses seven distinct categories of skin diseases. For our binary classification task, we focus on two classes: malignant melanoma (1114 images) and benign melanocytic nevi (6705 images). Some of the sample images from the HAM10000 dataset are illustrated in Fig. 4. The class IR between these two classes is 6.02. The images are in JPG format with an original resolution of 450 × 600 pixels. Each image is associated with metadata, providing crucial information, such as lesion type, patient demographics, and lesion location. To prepare the images for analysis, all are resized to 224 × 224 pixels and normalized to ensure pixel values fall within an appropriate range. Subsequently, the pretrained VGG16 model [38] is employed to extract deep features from the images. The extracted features are then flattened into a 1-D array to be used as input for the proposed RD-IFTSVM. To further enhance computational efficiency, principal component analysis is applied to lower the dimensionality of the attribute space.

A comparative performance analysis is performed to evaluate the proposed RD-IFTSVM against several baseline models for the binary classification of skin lesions. The evaluation is carried out using metrics, such as AUC, sensitivity, specificity, G-mean, and F -measure. The results of the experiments are presented in Table III. In the table, the bold entries represent the value of highest performance index corresponding to that column. The proposed RD-IFTSVM exhibited exceptional performance in classifying the skin lesions by achieving the highest AUC of 98.54%. CGFTSVM achieved an AUC of 97.71%, followed by IFTSVM- ID (94.89%), IFW-LSTSVM (93.23%), IFTPSVM (92.38%), TSVM (90.50%), ACFTSVM (90.00%), and SVM-SMOTE performs the least with an AUC of 72.75%. In addition, the proposed

TABLE III PERFORMANCE COMPARISON OF METHODS ON SKIN LESION CLASSIFICATION

RD-IFTSVM achieves a perfect sensitivity rate of 1, indicating its flawless detection of melanoma lesions (minority class), which is crucial for accurately diagnosing malignant lesions. The specificity rate is also high at 0.9708, reflecting the model’s effectiveness in identifying benign lesions (majority of cases). The G-mean and F -measure values of 0.9853 and 0.9194, respectively, further highlight the robustness of the proposed method. These results demonstrate the superior classification performance of the proposed technique compared to all baseline models, hence making it a highly effective approach for skin lesion classification.

This study introduces a novel relative density and nonmembership-based intuitionistic fuzzy twin support vector machine (RD-IFTSVM) to diminish the impact of noise, outliers, and imbalanced class distributions in classification tasks. The proposed RD-IFTSVM assesses the significance of each training pattern using relative density information derived from k-nearest neighbor distances. Furthermore, unlike conventional intuitionistic fuzzy-based models that solely utilize local information to calculate the nonmembership function, we define a new nonmembership function that utilizes two ratio-based measures to capture the global characteristics of the data. Through in-depth analysis, it is shown that this approach yields a more accurate and reliable evaluation of the credibility of training samples through the associated score function. Moreover,

the proposed RDNM-based membership function effectively addresses imbalanced datasets while simultaneously enhancing robustness to noise and outliers by reducing their impact significantly. Extensive experiments conducted on 30 benchmark KEEL and UCI datasets reveal that the proposed approach consistently outperforms existing baseline models. It achieved an exceptional average AUC of 91.63% with the linear kernel and 92.27% with the Gaussian kernel, highlighting its superior performance in handling imbalanced datasets. Furthermore, sensitivity analyses of the parameters, statistical analysis, and ablation studies are performed to thoroughly evaluate its performance. The proposed method is also applied to the HAM10000 dataset to showcase its real-world application in classifying skin lesions, proving to be an effective classifier for this task. Although the proposed method performs well on benchmark datasets, it may require further optimization for large-scale and high-dimensional datasets. In future work, we will evaluate its performance on multiclass classification problems, extending its

content: Abstract—To improve the robustness of SVM models to noise and outliers, fuzzy support vector machine (FSVM) has been proposed. However, many existing FSVM models have limitations such as their dependence on assumptions, limited optimization, and unreasonable handling of noise. To address these problems, we propose a novel approach called curriculum learning-based FSVM. Our approach employs a curriculum-learning strategy, where model initially learns easy samples to avoid noise interference and obtain a good initial solution, before proceeding to learn all samples, including hard ones. To distinguish between easy and hard samples, we introduce an adaptive density-based clustering model and it is extended to kernel feature space. Moreover, we propose a slack variable-based fuzzy membership function to evaluate the importance of samples. Additionally, our model adaptively adapts the importance of samples based on feedback during the learning process. Finally, our experimental results on popular benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed model outperforms existing competitors in terms of accuracy and robustness. Index Terms—fuzzy support vector machine, curriculum learning strategy, noise, density-based clustering, slack variable

content: S UPPORT vector machine (SVM) [1] has been widely applied in various fields, due to its solid mathematical background, high generalization capability, and ability to find global classification solutions [2]. Even though SVM has achieved great success, it still has drawbacks. For example, it considers all samples equally important and ignores dealing with noise and outliers [3], [4], which makes it sensitive to noise or outliers. According to the design ideas of fuzzy membership functions, they can be summarized into three strategies, namely, hyperplane-based FSVM [2], [6], [7], clustering-based FSVM [8], [9], [10], [11], [12], [13] and k-nearest neighborsbased FSVM [14], [15], [16]. Their idea is to emphasize important samples, thereby alleviating the effect of noise and outliers on SVM. Specifically, the hyperplane-based FSVM judges importance of the sample based on the distance from the sample to hyperplane. The farther the sample is from the hyperplane, the lower the importance. For example, Liu [7] proposed a hyperplane-based Gaussian fuzzy function that can assign the fuzzy membership degree of the sample according to the distance from samples to hyperplane. The clusteringbased FSVM judges importance of the sample based on its similarity to the overall samples within the same class. The higher the similarity between a sample and the overall samples, the greater its importance. For example,
doc_title: Curriculum Learning-Based Fuzzy Support Vector Machine

content: Hazarika and Gupta [13] proposed using support vector data description (SVDD) model [17] to evaluate the affinity of majority class sample. Yang et. al [18] proposed a clustering-based Gaussian fuzzy function that can assign the fuzzy membership of samples according to their distance from the cluster centers. The k-nearest neighbors-based FSVM judges importance of the sample based on its similarity with the surrounding samples. The higher the similarity, the higher the importance. For example, Fan et al. [19] proposed entropy-based FSVM. It can analyze the entropy in local regions to judge the importance of samples. Chen et al. [16] proposed using graph learning to evaluate the similarity between sample points and surrounding samples. However, these models still have some limitations. Some of these limitations include 1) Dependence on Assumption: They are based on the assumption that the process of judging the importance of samples is not affected by noise samples. However, this may not always hold in real-world situations, on the contrary,
doc_title: Curriculum Learning-Based Fuzzy Support Vector Machine

content: noise samples or outliers often disrupt our judgments or model’s, making it more challenging to assess the importance of samples accurately. 2) Limited Optimization: Many existing fuzzy membership functions are heuristic [20] and cannot be optimized in the learning process of the model. This limitation makes it difficult to find a great solution, which affects the accuracy of the model. 3) Unreasonable Handing of Noise samples: The hyperplane-based FSVM emphasizes the samples close to the hyperplane, however, the area between classes is very fuzzy and may contain noise samples. Emphasizing samples in the fuzzy area may not be conducive to enhancing the performance of the model. To tackle the aforementioned issues, we present fuzzy SVM
doc_title: Curriculum Learning-Based Fuzzy Support Vector Machine

content: based on curriculum learning [21]. In particular, we first embed the idea of curriculum learning into the FSVM model. Specifically, new models can first learn easy samples to obtain a great initial solution, and then learn all samples (including hard samples) to ensure that all information is learned. Additionally, they can adaptively adjust the importance of samples at different stages. These learning processes are similar to human learning in courses. Moreover, we propose slack variablebased fuzzy membership functions to reasonably evaluate noise and outliers. In summary, the main contributions of our work are: • Novel curriculum learning-based FSVM models are proposed. They can more accurately evaluate the importance of samples at an initial stage and then constantly adjust these evaluations based on learning feedback. • Novel slack variable-based fuzzy membership functions are proposed. This approach can evaluate the importance of samples more reasonably, thereby obtaining more reliable results. • A density clustering algorithm is optimized so that it can be data-driven and adjust parameters adaptively. It is adopted to distinguish between easy samples and hard ones and it is extended to kernel feature space.

content: DBSCAN is a widely used density-based clustering algorithm that is capable of identifying clusters of arbitrary shapes in a dataset. To identify clusters, DBSCAN relies on two important parameters: the radius ϵ and the minimum number of points required to form a dense region, minP ts [26]. The algorithm starts by selecting an arbitrary data point and identifies all other points within a distance ϵ. If the number of points within ϵ is greater than or equal to minP ts, then the selected point is considered a core object. The algorithm then identifies all other points within ϵ of the core object and adds them to the same cluster. This process continues until no
section_path: B. Density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise
doc_title: Curriculum Learning-Based Fuzzy Support Vector Machine

content: more points can be added to the cluster. Any points that are not within ϵ of a core object are classified as noise or outliers. In summary, DBSCAN is a powerful clustering algorithm and has the following advantages: • Ability to handle clusters of arbitrary shapes and sizes: It can identify clusters of any shape, as it does not assume any particular shape of clusters. This means that it can identify clusters with irregular shapes and broken structures [27]. • Fewer parameters: It does not need to know the number of clusters in prior [27]. • Robustness to noise: DBSCAN is robust to noise in the data. It can identify noise samples or outliers and exclude them from the clusters [28]. • Efficiency: DBSCAN has a time complexity of O(nlogn) and can process large datasets efficiently [26], [27]. However, it is sensitive to parameters ϵ and minP ts. Additionally, it only applies to the original input space. In our work,

content: To solve dependence on assumption and limited optimization problems of FSVM, we formulate the curriculum learningbased FSVM. Curriculum learning strategy includes learning easy samples and then learning hard ones. In addition, it also includes an iterative learning strategy. Its algorithm steps are described in Fig. 3 and Algorithm 2. Specifically, the algorithm first divides the data into positive and negative classes (X+ and X−) according to their label. Next, the ADBSCAN algorithm analyzes the two classes of data separately and identifies easy samples and hard ones. The purpose of analyzing each class independently is to avoid interference from different classes. Then, the standard SVM is trained in the easy samples to obtain the initial hyperplane, which allows model to obtain a high-quality initial solution. Next, the fuzzy membership degree for all samples (including hard samples) can be obtained through the initial hyperplane and slack variable-based fuzzy membership function. The reason for using the all samples is to avoid missing data information. Finally, iterative learning

Our models, FSVM1-SIC, FSVM2- SIC, FSVM3-SIC, and FSVM4-SIC are regarded as the control methods, while their respective pre-improved models and SVM are employed as the compared models. In this test, a significant difference between our models and compared models is distinguished by the critical distance (CD), and (cid:112) CD = q (k(k + 1)/6N ) where k denotes the number of α compared models and N denotes the number of datasets. For Bonferroni-Dunn test, q = 2.459 at significance level α α = 0.1, then CD = 1.296 (k = 5, N = 18). Otherwise, any unconnected methods are considered to have significantly different classification performance with our models. Based on the TABLE V, TABLE VI, and Fig. (7) and Fig. (8), we can draw the following conclusions: • Regardless of whether linear kernel or Gaussian kernel is used, the curriculum learning-based model consistently achieves better classification rankings than the models under other strategies. This may be because the curriculum learning-based models can obtain better initial solution (initial hyperplane) when learning easy samples. In addition, learning hard samples ensures the integrity of the training data. These results support our theoretical hypotheses. • Compared with traditional FSVM, FSVMs that incorporate an iterative learning strategy generally achieve better classification rankings, but their advantages are not obvious. This may be because iterative learning strategy do not obtain a high-quality initial solution (initial hyperplane) like curriculum learning-based FSVM. When the initial solution is good,

Abstract—Traditional fuzzy set methods, designed around the finest granularity of inputsa˛łindividual points and their membership degreesa˛łoften struggle with inefficiencies and label noise. To overcome these challenges, we have introduced granular-ball computing into the fuzzy set, creating the new granular-ball fuzzy set framework. This approach uses granularball inputs rather than single points, significantly reducing the number of entities and minimizing susceptibility to the noise affecting individual sample points. As a result, our framework enhances both efficiency and robustness compared to traditional methods and is applicable across various domains of fuzzy data processing. Furthermore, we have applied this framework to fuzzy support vector machines (FSVM), developing the Granular-ball Fuzzy Support Vector Machine (GBFSVM). Experimental tests on UCI benchmark datasets show that GBFSVM surpasses traditional models in efficiency and robustness. The source codes and datasets are both available on the public link: http://www.cquptshuyinxia.com/GBFSVM.html, https://github.com/syxiaa/GBFS. Index Terms—Fuzzy set, granular-ball, SVM, granular computing, classification, label noise, robust.

Recognizing the value of these fuzzy phenomena, American computer and cybernetics expert Professor L.A. Zadeh introduced the concept of fuzzy sets in

Since its introduction [50], fuzzy set theory has been widely applied in diverse fields such as control systems [54], pattern recognition [6], and machine learning [40]. This has spurred advancements in fuzzy rough sets, leading to significant research and applications in feature selection [18], [37], [38], [45], clustering [14], [26], [23], image retrieval [11], and decision making [34], [53], among other areas [5], [4], [9], [13], [24]. In considering the classification problem of fuzzy data sets, Lin et al. [20] proposed a model known as the fuzzy support vector machine (FSVM), which uses fuzzy membership to each input point. While this model effectively utilizes sample information, the training stage’s complexity remains high for a large number of data classification problems. content: The aforementioned methods are based on the finest granularity of inputs within granular computing [51], [52], as depicted in Fig. 1(a). This level of detail, while precise, often results in reduced efficiency and robustness. In contrast, human cognition operates on a “global-first” rule, with the visual system particularly attuned to global topological characteristics. This cognitive approach processes information from large, coarse-grained structures to smaller, fine-grained details, as illustrated in Fig. 2 [41]. For instance, humans first perceive the broad shapes of the letters “H” and “S” before discerning the finer details that compose them. In granular computing, opting for larger granularity sizes can enhance efficiency and robustness against noise, albeit at the potential cost of losing detailed information. Conversely, smaller granularity focuses more on detail but may compromise efficiency and robustness against label noise. Over the past decades,

content: researchers globally have extensively studied the granulation of vast datasets and knowledge into varying sizes based on specific tasks [21], [28], [29], [55]. These granularities and their interrelations are then leveraged to address diverse problems [3], [8], [36], [48]. Selecting appropriate granularities for different scenarios can significantly improve the performance of multi-granularity learning methods and effectively solve practical challenges [27], [35], [49]. Therefore, Xia et al. [42] proposed granular-ball classifiers using some hyper-balls to granulate the dataset into granularballs of different sizes [43]. The granular-ball support vector machine (GBSVM) [44], a further development, has higher accuracy and efficiency than the traditional SVM. content: integrating granular-ball computing, we present the following key contributions in this paper: • We propose a framework called the granular-ball fuzzy set, which defines the membership of granular-balls and introduces the concept of fuzzy granular-balls, making it different from traditional fuzzy data processing methods. • The granular-ball fuzzy support vector machine model (GBFSVM) with granular-balls as input instead of sample points is derived based on the fuzzy granular-ball framework and FSVM in detail. • The granular-ball fuzzy set framework is applied to classification problems with triangular fuzzy number characteristics. This paper uses the possibility measure theory to derive the GBFSVM model based on triangular fuzzy numbers in detail. • We employ an approximation function to solve the GB- SVM using the sequential minimal optimization (SMO) algorithm. Experimental results show that GBFSVM surpasses the traditional SVM and FSVM in terms of both robustness and effectiveness. The rest of this paper is organized as follows: we introduce the concepts of fuzzy sets and the work related to granularball computing in section II. Section III details the granularball fuzzy set framework and the definition of fuzzy granularball. Section IV introduces the implement of the granularball fuzzy set in fuzzy support vector machines and support vector machines based on triangular fuzzy numbers. The experimental results and analysis are presented in Section V. Finally, some conclusions and future work are provided in Section VI.

content: As modern science and technology advance, the complexity of systems we engage with increases, particularly in the humanities, social sciences, and other "soft science" fields. In these areas, making precise evaluations can be challenging due to constraints in cognitive resources or the availability of information during decision-making. In scenarios involving multiattribute decision-making where detailed decision information is scarce, decision-makers often struggle to accurately evaluate the available options. Consequently, the concept of fuzzy sets becomes essential, which is characterized as follows: Definition 1. content: In this section, due to the difficulty in procuring suitable data with triangular fuzzy number characteristics, we limit our experiments to the implement of FSVM method for fuzzy granular-ball extensions. Furthermore, as the approximation function is utilized to address the problem using the SMO method, this study also conducts a comparison with the algorithm that employs the FSVM approach when the radius is set to zero. In the experiment, we utilize Definition 8, and employ the simplest membership degree function (12) to obtain the membership degree of the center point. This degree is then used as the membership degree of granular-balls for the experimental implementation. The feasibility and efficiency of GBFSVM are verified by comparison with the SVM, FSVM, CDFTSVM [7] and DC-IFLSTSVM models [12]. In the experiment, our hardware experimental environment is AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 5975WX 32-Cores 3.60 GHz, and the software experiment environment is Python 3.9. content: In this study, we selected datasets as depicted in Table I for comparative experimentation, setting the parameter C = 1. Each dataset was divided into training and testing subsets in an 8:2 ratio. For each dataset, we chose the optimal model based on the evaluation of the training set and then input the test set to obtain results. Experimental results of GBFSVM, FSVM, SVM, CDFTSVM and DC-IFLSTSVM represent the average outcomes of four runs on each dataset. Additionally, we compared the GBFSVM model with R=0 and the center point set as input. In the experiment, we tested each dataset under different percentages of label noise, including 0%, 5%, 10%, 15%, 20%, 25% and 30%. Notably, we introduced different levels of noise only to the training set, not the test set. The classification accuracies of SVM, FSVM, CDFTSVM, DC-IFLSTSVM, GBFSVM and GBFSVM (R=0)

content: under different noise levels are listed in Table II. The most accurate algorithm on each dataset is marked in boldface. The results demonstrate that the four models of SVM, FSVM, CDFTSVM and DC-IFLSTSVM have unstable accuracy changes. GBFSVM or GBFSVM (R=0) achieves a higher classification accuracy than SVM, FSVM, CDFTSVM and DC-IFLSTSVM in most instances. Interestingly, in some scenarios, the GBFSVM model performs better when the radius is 0. This can be attributed to certain inaccuracies in the approximate function solution. By setting the radius of all granular-balls to zero, we replace the entire ball with its center point as the input. While this input form resembles that of the FSVM, the center point set differs from the original dataset, thus preserving robustness. Consequently, the classification accuracy of the GNBSVM model generally surpasses that of the FSVM model. Notably,

content: GBFSVM consistently outperforms other models at high noise levels. This is because the label of each fuzzy granular-ball is defined as the most frequently occurring label within the ball, and appropriately lowering the purity threshold can diminish the impact of label noise. Furthermore, even when the radius is 0, the model maintains a certain level of robustness.

content: To further verify the high efficiency of granular-ball fuzzy set, we provide the running time results for SVM, FSVM, GBFSVM and GBFSVM (R=0) solved by the SMO algorithm in Table III. The bold numbers is the best results of the four methods. The time of the granular-ball purity threshold optimization was not considered, and the average running time of GBFSVM was used in this experiment. It is obvious that GBSVM is much faster than the other two methods. The reason is that the implement of granular-balls instead of points as input greatly reduces the number of training samples, which trains the data faster. A detailed theoretical analysis is presented in Section II. We excluded the CDFTSVM and DC-IFLSTSVM models from our time comparison as they were not tested after converting points into granular-balls. In future work, these two models can combine the granularball computing to yield more efficient and robust results. In summary, the GBFSVM is much more efficient than SVM and FSVM.

content: This paper systematically defines the concept of fuzzy granular-balls and proposes a scalable, efficient, and robust fuzzy big data processing algorithm framework, which significantly reduces the time and space complexity associated with existing fuzzy classifiers. Importantly, this framework is applicable to all fuzzy data processing methods. This study integrated the particle fuzzy set framework into FSVM to develop the GBFSVM model and the corresponding model based on triangular fuzzy numbers, thereby improving the classification accuracy and speeding up the classification. However, our approach does have certain limitations. This study uses the SMO algorithm to solve the approximate function, b ut the model solution obtained is not the most accurate. How to accurately and efficiently solve the GBFSVM dual model deserves further exploration in future research. Moreover, we have not used the triangular fuzzy number-based GBFSVM model in real-world scenarios. As part of our future research agenda, we also need to apply the spherical fuzzy set framework to more existing computational methods for processing big data to improve processing efficiency.

content: Zhenlei Wu, Xiao :IOD School of Computer Science and Technology, Mianyan | EEEI wuzhenlei0215@mails.swust.edu.cn, xqpanu 5202© 00.13$/52/9-2356-5133-8-979 Abstract—Fuzzy support vector machine (FSVM) effectively enhances the model’s robustness to common noise and outliers by introducing a sample membership mechanism. To further improve the model’s performance in complex scenarios such as data poisoning and adversarial noise, researchers have proposed the curriculum learning-based fuzzy support vector machine (CLFSVM), which optimizes the training process through a curriculum learning strategy. However, the performance of this model heavily depends on the quality of the initial core sample set, and an improper initial selection can lead to a significant | )moCtsurT( degradation in model performance. To address this issue, we propose an innovative framework, the granular ball and curriculum learning-based FSVM (GB-CLFSVM), which includes three key components. First,

it constructs a multi-stage training paradigm from easy to hard based on curriculum learning snoitacinummoC theory, ensuring the model gradually adapts to complex data distributions. Second, it employs granular balls to automatically select a set of core samples, building a small and high-quality training set and generating a robust standard SVM as the initialization baseline for FSVM. Finally, it designs an adaptive composite weighting mechanism to dynamically calculate sample dna fuzzy memberships. By comprehensively considering local sample gnitupmoC density and class information, this mechanism assigns fine-grained weights to samples of varying complexity, thereby optimizing the iterative process of curriculum learning. Experimental results show that GB-CLFSVM significantly outperforms the CLFSVM baseline model in both classification accuracy and noise resistance, ni ycavirP demonstrating exceptional generalization ability, especially in data scenarios with noisy features and labels. Support vector machine (SVM) [1], [2] is widely regarded ,tsurT as a classification tool with excellent generalization ability. However, in real-world scenarios, data often contains noise and no ecnerefnoC outliers due to measurement errors, environmental interference, or transmission issues, which are difficult to eliminate completely through preprocessing techniques. SVM has inherent drawbacks when dealing with noisy data, as it treats all training lanoitanretnI samples equally. This allows noise and outliers to have the same impact on the decision hyperplane as normal samples. Such an equalized treatment leads to two consequences. First, as the number of noisy samples increases, the localization ht42 error of the hyperplane accumulates, causing a shift in the EEEI * The corresponding author.

Fuzzy support vector machine (FSVM) [3] offered a new solution to this problem. By assigning different membership values to each training sample, FSVM can effectively reduce the impact of noisy samples on classification performance. Recently, researchers have made significant progress in improving FSVM. One line of research focuses on directly enhancing robustness by refining the membership function or the model architecture. Liu et al. [4] improved the membership function to focus on handling noisy samples in the boundary region, thereby enhancing classification accuracy. Chen et al. [5] proposed the NFTSVM framework to balance efficiency with generalization ability. Tanveer et al. [6] introduced an energy parameter and a regularization term to simultaneously improve both robustness and training speed. Yu et al. [7] and Tao et al. [8] utilized relative sample density and affinity information to adjust membership degrees,

effectively mitigating the class imbalance problem. Another approach involves indirectly optimizing model robustness through preprocessing or hybrid modeling. Liu et al. [9] proposed a FSVM that utilizes support vector data description for robust intrusion detection. Li et al. [10] employed a genetic algorithm and fuzzy c-means (FCM) to optimize the handling of high-dimensional data. These methods have demonstrated good performance in environments with common noise. However, those FSVM models still exhibit significant vulnerability when faced with carefully crafted data poisoning attacks [11]. Attackers can significantly degrade the model’s classification performance by simply injecting minor perturbations into the feature space or tampering with a few training sample labels. For example, after adding slight noise to the features of moon dataset, the decision boundary of FSVM becomes distorted, as shown in Fig. 1(b), from its originally smooth state in Fig. 1(a). This comparison visually reveals the fundamental shortcomings of existing methods in resisting noise. To address these challenges,

researchers have begun to explore more robust solutions. Ju et al. [12] integrated kernel grey relational analysis into FSVM, demonstrating the algorithm’s superior performance in noisy scenarios. Granular ball

computing (GBC), proposed by Xia et al. [13], [14], identifies noise through spatial coverage and has shown outstanding performance in models such as SVM and FSVM. These methods, through different technical paths, have all enhanced the model’s ability to resist noise to some extent. Curriculum learning [15]–[17] has opened another path for robustness research in machine learning. Then, Chen et al. [18] applied the concept of curriculum learning to FSVM (CLFSVM), using clustering to obtain high-quality samples and implementing a multistage training strategy. This allows the model to first learn basic features from relatively easy samples and then gradually adapt to more difficult data. However, the CLFSVM exhibits vulnerability in core sample selection. If the initial training set is contaminated with noise, the entire learning process can be severely compromised. This problem is particularly pronounced in adversarial environments. Based on the preceding analysis,

we integrate the noise identification capability of granular ball computing with the progressive training strategy of curriculum learning. We propose the granular ball and curriculum learning-based fuzzy support vector machine (GB-CLFSVM) framework to enhance the robustness of FSVM. Preliminary experimental results indicate that this integrated approach demonstrates significant advantages in noise resistance. The main contributions of this work are as follows: • The GB-CLFSVM framework is developed, which adopts a progressive curriculum learning strategy to realize multistage training. This framework starts with easy samples to establish an initial decision boundary, and then gradually introduces complex samples (including noisy samples), thus avoiding the problem that traditional methods use the entire training set in each iteration, which causes noisy samples to interfere with the learning process. • We designed a density-based granular ball algorithm to automatically select a “small but high-quality” set of core samples. These core samples are then used to train a standard SVM,

providing an initial solution for the FSVM model in the subsequent curriculum learning process. • We proposed an adaptive composite weighting mechanism for fuzzy membership. By considering local sample density and class information, this mechanism dynamically assigns fine-grained weights to different samples. This approach maintains the model’s sensitivity to clean samples
while effectively suppressing the negative impact of noisy ones.

By assigning a distinct membership value to each training sample, FSVM intelligently differentiates the importance of each sample. Specifically, reliable samples have a dominant influence on the formation of the decision boundary, while the impact of samples suspected to be noise or outliers is reduced. This strategy offers a dual advantage. On one hand, it retains the core characteristics of the standard SVM, including the structural risk minimization principle and the ability to handle non-linear problems using kernel functions. On the other hand, it significantly enhances the model’s robustness in noisy environments, allowing it to maintain both high classification accuracy for high-dimensional data and strong anti-interference capabilities. Although ADBSCAN enhances the robustness of CLFSVM in noisy scenarios, it still suffers from the following limitations. First, the assumption of setting ϵ to the global average distance is overly restrictive. If the data contains multiple clusters with significantly different densities (e.g., the coexistence of highdensity and low-density clusters), a large ϵ can cause clusters that should be separate to be incorrectly merged, while a small ϵ can lead to clusters in sparse regions being misclassified as noise. Second, ADBSCAN returns all points that satisfy the local density condition to form the core samples, but its size can be excessively large. This redundancy weakens the “from

content: The granular ball algorithm proposed by Xia et al. [20] innovatively uses hyperspheres to represent data granules and has been successfully applied to various classification models. Specifically, the algorithm determines the ball’s center by the centroid of the samples and calculates its radius as the average distance from the samples to the center, thereby enhancing its noise resistance. Additionally, the generation of granular balls employs a dynamic splitting strategy based on 2-means clustering and a purity threshold. However, this method is designed for multi-class scenarios and does not adequately consider the characteristics of single-class samples. To address this issue, we propose a density-based granular ball algorithm. Its core idea is to establish a dynamic splitting mechanism controlled by a density threshold θ, while prioritizing the retention of stable sub-clusters in high-density regions to achieve automatic selection of high-quality samples. This elite strategy ensures that the base SVM model is constructed from the most reliable and representative prototypes, aligning

In line 1, the parameters are initialized, it treats the entire set of samples as a single initial macrogranular ball. During the iterative splitting phase (lines 2-13), a while-loop is used to dynamically partition the granular balls. In each iteration, if a granular ball’s density falls below the predefined threshold θ and it contains at least two samples, it is split into two smaller sub-balls. This process continues until all granular balls meet the density requirement or are too small to be split further. In the core sample selection phase (lines 14-18), a for-loop iterates through the final granular balls. For each high-density ball that meets the threshold, the sample closest to its geometric center is selected as a core sample and added to the core sample set D . content: To validate the effectiveness of the density-based granular ball algorithm for selecting core sample in GB- CLFSVM, we designed a comparative experiment. We used the ‘make moons’ synthetic dataset, which exhibits typical non-convex characteristics, consisting of 300 samples and two classes. After standardization, Gaussian noise N (0, 0.22) was added. We compared the core sample selection performance of GB-CLFSVM (with a density threshold θ = 2.5) against CLFSVM (with its adaptive ϵ and minPts parameters). The experimental results, shown in Fig. 3, reveal two key findings. First, although the ADBSCAN algorithm could identify highdensity regions, the 300 core samples it produced were significantly redundant and failed to reflect the sample filtering characteristic required for curriculum learning. In contrast, our granular ball algorithm selected only 13 core samples (4.33% of the total) that were located at the centers of highdensity regions, which are spatially independent and highly representative. Second, through precise control of the density threshold θ (set based on data scale analysis), our algorithm achieved a “small but high-quality” sample selection (a 95.67% reduction in the number of core samples), thereby constructing an ideal training sequence for the subsequent curriculum learning. These findings confirm the advantages of the granular ball algorithm in feature space sampling, as the core sample set it generates not only preserves the data distribution characteristics but also effectively reduces training complexity.

content: To further evaluate the generalization performance of GB- CLFSVM, we conducted comparative experiments using the Gaussian kernel function, with parameter settings identical to those used for the linear kernel. As shown in Table IV, the results confirm the effectiveness of GB-CLFSVM. First, GB- CLFSVM achieved a best performance rate of 88.24% (on 15 out of 17 datasets), significantly higher than CLFSVM’s 11.76% (2 out of 17). Its average rank (2.83–3.67) was also markedly better than that of CLFSVM (5.14–6.28). Second, GB-CLFSVM surpassed 90% accuracy on five datasets, including “vote”, while CLFSVM’s highest accuracy was only 88.14%. More importantly, although the performance of both algorithms decreased on some datasets with the Gaussian kernel, GB-CLFSVM’s accuracy on the Coil20 dataset dropped from 91.67% to 77.78% (a 13.89% decrease), whereas CLFSVM’s plummeted from 86.46% to 5.07% (an 81.39% decrease). This disparity was also evident on datasets like Jaffe and Yale, indicating that GB-CLFSVM possesses more stable kernel adaptability and stronger noise robustness, with its performance being far less affected by the choice of kernel function than CLFSVM.

content: To enhance the robustness of FSVM in complex scenarios such as data poisoning and adversarial noise, this paper proposes the GB-CLFSVM framework. It enhances model performance through three aspects. First, it constructs a multi-stage and easy-to-hard training paradigm based on curriculum learning theory, ensuring the model gradually adapts to complex data distributions. Second, it employs a granular ball algorithm for the automatic selection of core samples, building a initial training set based on the “small but high-quality” principle, and trains a robust standard SVM as the initialization baseline for FSVM. Finally, it innovatively proposes an adaptive composite weighting mechanism that dynamically optimizes the calculation of fuzzy memberships by comprehensively considering the inherent classification ambiguity of samples, the impact of the iterative process on the model, and their relative positions in the feature space. Experiment results in noisy scenarios demonstrate that GB-CLFSVM significantly outperforms existing baseline models in terms of classification accuracy, noise resistance, and kernel function generalization ability, thereby validating the effectiveness and advancement of the proposed method.In future work, we will extend our method to more complex scenarios and compare it with stateof-the-art models to further validate its effectiveness.
